issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Sister Margaret had always found solace in her faith and her community at the convent. But everything changed on that fateful day when her younger brother, a firefighter, was killed in a tragic accident while responding to an emergency call. She vividly remembered receiving the news from her tearful sister-in-law, feeling as though she'd been punched in the gut. As the days turned into weeks, Sister Margaret began to question whether she could have done something to prevent his death. "If only I had prayed harder," she would tell herself, or "maybe if I had been more supportive when he was going through tough times." These thoughts of self-blame and failure to protect her brother swirled in her mind like a vortex, making it hard for her to concentrate on her daily prayers and duties. She started performing mental rituals to ward off any potential harm that might befall those she loved - counting the rosary beads a certain number of times before bed or silently reciting specific psalms whenever she felt anxious. These attempts at magical prevention were, in part, an attempt to regain control over her life and calm the gnawing feeling that she couldn't rely on herself. "What if I'm not doing enough to keep others safe?" she'd wonder. As a result of these fears, Sister Margaret started avoiding anything that reminded her of her brother - his favorite hymns during Mass, visiting their childhood home, or even looking at old family photos. She became increasingly withdrawn from community activities and found herself performing rituals even in the midst of important tasks, hoping to stave off any potential calamity. However, despite these efforts, memories of that terrible day would still burst into her consciousness without warning - triggered by something as simple as a red fire truck driving down the street or the faint scent of smoke wafting through the air. When this happened, Sister Margaret's mind would replay every excruciating detail: the anguish on her sister-in-law's face, the helpless feeling of being unable to prevent his death, and the haunting sound of sirens echoing in the distance. These memories, so vivid and clear in some moments yet frustratingly blank in others, seemed to taunt Sister Margaret - forcing her to confront all that she couldn't control or change. They also reinforced her maladaptive strategies; for example, after being triggered by a particular image, she might spend hours reenacting the events surrounding her brother's death in an attempt to rewrite history. Her mental rituals and avoidance behaviors became self-reinforcing loops - with memories fueling more magical thinking and negative appraisals driving increased reliance on these coping mechanisms. As time passed, Sister Margaret noticed that her relationships within the convent began to suffer as well. She found it difficult to engage in discussions about faith or provide guidance when needed, fearing she wasn't worthy of leading others due to her own feelings of inadequacy and self-blame. Feeling increasingly isolated, she realized that these coping mechanisms were no longer tenable - they had become a prison preventing her from moving forward. It was this recognition that finally brought Sister Margaret to seek help - the fear of losing herself in her grief and inability to reconnect with the very faith that once comforted her now overshadowing all else. She was afraid that without change, these loops would consume her completely, leaving behind only a hollow shell of the compassionate nun she once aspired to be.
